title: Short Stuff: The Iowa Caucus
summary: Short Stuff episode published February 5, 2020, the day after the 2020 Iowa caucus, which was marred by problems with the reporting app and delayed results. Josh and Chuck explain what a caucus is, how Democratic caucusgoers show support by standing in designated corners of a room and the viability threshold, the Republican approach (regular primary-style voting), and the failed plan for virtual caucuses rejected by the DNC over hacking concerns. They discuss why Iowa became first in the nation in 1972 (a GOP thirty-day notice rule and a hotel booking problem pushed the caucus earlier), Iowa and New Hampshire state laws keeping them first, the media's outsized role in creating front-runners and dark horses, past results such as George McGovern in 1972, Jimmy Carter's 1976 showing behind uncommitted, Bill Clinton in 1992, and Barack Obama in 2008, and the idea that Iowa's importance is artificial and self-fulfilling.

segments.title: Newsy episode on the Iowa caucus
segments.summary: Hosts introduce a timely episode recorded the day after the Iowa caucus, noting the results were delayed and the caucus was a mess.

segments.title: What a caucus is and how Democrats caucus
segments.summary: Definition of a caucus as a meeting of party members. Democratic caucusgoers stand in a section of the room for their candidate; a candidate needs about 15 percent of the room to be viable, otherwise supporters must join another group or go home. Republicans vote like a regular primary.

segments.title: Failed app and virtual caucus plan
segments.summary: Iowa planned virtual caucuses, which the DNC rejected over hacking risk. A reporting app used to tally delegates malfunctioned, though accounts differ on whether it crashed, and the hosts note speculation about Russia.

segments.title: Results timing and tie-breaking
segments.summary: Results were usually known the morning after but were delayed this year, with a release promised by 5 pm Eastern. Ties were broken by coin toss and a name drawn from a hat.

segments.title: Why Iowa is first and its artificial importance
segments.summary: Iowa is not very diverse and the caucus is largely rural and white. Its importance comes from media attention. Iowa became first in 1972 because a GOP thirty-day notice rule and a hotel booking problem pushed the caucus earlier; Iowa then passed a state law to stay first, and New Hampshire has a state law to hold the first primary.

segments.title: Media influence, front-runners and historical results
segments.summary: The media's labels such as front-runner and dark horse, and its poll releases or withholding, shape voting and funding. Winning Iowa is not required: a third-place finish has preceded nomination, Clinton placed third in 1992, and McGovern placed first but did not win the presidency. Carter was beaten by uncommitted in 1976. Obama's 2008 Iowa win launched his campaign.

segments.title: Artificial bump and candidate claims of victory
segments.summary: The hosts describe Iowa's importance as self-fulfilling, citing Glenn Greenwald's point that the expected bump did not come. Candidates claimed victory, and uncommitted voters in the gym outnumbered some candidates.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts close the episode, noting the caucus might not be around next time, and give the show's production credit.
